Cult.fit builds operational muscle with Codex
Cult.fit is using Codex to help teams across functions build tools, move faster, and change how work gets done.
20+
internal applications built by non-engineering teams in recent months
$100,000+
annual software savings by rebuilding an internal capability with Codex
50%+

Cult.fit is one of India’s leading technology-enabled fitness companies, operating 708 fitness centers across 77 cities and serving nearly one million paid members. Its business combines subscription-based access to gyms and trainer-led fitness classes with a growing consumer products portfolio spanning fitness equipment, accessories, workout footwear and activewear.
As the company grew, it wanted to solve more operational and product challenges without adding layers of process and complexity. By standardizing engineering on Codex and then extending it beyond engineering, cult.fit is helping teams across the organization analyze data, build tools, and move ideas into production. Alongside its Codex rollout, it is using the OpenAI API to develop more personalized member experiences, including through its AI Trainer.
For Santhosh Kumar, CTO at cult.fit, AI presented an opportunity to change how the organization works. “We wanted to become more AI-native in the way we run things,” he says. “How can we run our operations or transform our operations to be AI-first? What new customer experiences can we offer? And how can we transform how we run our organization?”
Cult.fit’s first major shift was in engineering. Before standardizing on Codex, developers were using a mix of coding agents and assistants. Different tools meant different conventions for repositories, agent instructions, skills, and development workflows, making it harder to share knowledge and reuse capabilities across teams.
Cult.fit wanted a shared platform around which it could standardize the software development lifecycle. The company chose Codex as that foundation. Repository structures, skills, testing, code review, and feedback loops could now follow common conventions across teams.
“Once we standardized on Codex, we could build our software development lifecycle around a single platform.”
The team then extended Codex into more specialized engineering workflows. Its Site Reliability Engineering agent can aggregate information from observability platforms and logs, investigate incidents, and, in many cases, create a pull request with a proposed fix for an engineer to review. Security agents help identify and address vulnerabilities, while other on-call agents investigate recurring production issues.
Cult.fit is also moving toward a more fully spec-driven development model, where a specification can guide work through the software development lifecycle toward a pull request for an engineer to review. This gives teams a more repeatable path from a defined requirement to working code.

news.summary: OpenAI’s Codex is being adopted by Cult.fit to streamline internal application development across non-engineering teams, reducing costs and speeding tool creation. news.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
news.source_text:
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.
Here’s an overview of what’s new:
Fast and cost-effective at scale
Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
Longer clips up to 15 seconds
You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.
Better reference adherence
You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.
Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.
More consistent results
You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.
Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.
Easier editing in conversation
You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, mak
news.summary: Google DeepMind has launched Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, a new video generation model that supports up to 15-second clips, multi-turn conversational editing, and tighter reference adherence, all at a 30% lower price. This upgrade makes high‑quality, brand‑consistent video content more affordable and easier to produce for business users via the Gemini API.

S2: Leveraging the lower cost and conversational editing can reduce time‑to‑market for training and promotional content, but missing out could delay your team’s ability to create dynamic video assets quickly. news.title: Underdog shows off a 32MB speech model in new demo
news.summary_raw: Despite its small size, Underdog's new model can generate both speech and music.
news.source_text:
AI companies across the world are racing to make bigger and better models, but the problem is all of them need massive amounts of processing power. On the other end, some researchers and startups are creating smaller models that can run on edge devices, like your phone or computer.
One such startup, Underdog, has released a game built with its new voice model called Woof that’s only 32MB large.
The game features a room with a retro tech theme, a typewriter, and a CRT monitor. There is a desk lamp, which makes a sound when you click its switch. The intro warns users about “intrusive” cloud providers in the town — ostensibly a jab at cloud-based models.
You can interact with the typewriter and music tuner.
You can type anything on the typewriter using your keyboard, and the game will speak it back. You can also rotate the tuner to generate different kinds of music.
All of this works within the browser through Underdog’s speech generation model, which, the company says, can run on most devices without any internet connection. The model has 31 million parameters and is open for everyone to download.
While such a small model likely won’t replace bigger models, it may still be enough to drive local assistant experiences or create personalized podcasts.
This demo comes weeks after Underdog launched Bark, a 167 MB speech-to-text model also designed to run on edge devices for transcription and dictation.
Sigil Wen, the founder of Underdog, told TechCrunch that he started building the app because, instead of using notetakers like Granola, he wanted to build his own system with AI models that can run on users’ devices and let them own their data.
“I think we will be able to run most capable models of today on the devices you already own within months. We just want to train the best open models that are American-made, that are open, that are capable and allow people to have private AI,” he said, referring to his manifesto.
In addition to the two voice models mentioned above, Underdog has also released a 27-billion-parameter model that can run on laptops, along with a waitlisted app that the company is positioning as a locally-hosted alternative to Muse and Instinct.
news.summary: Underdog has released a 32 MB voice model called Woof that runs entirely on local devices, enabling offline speech generation in browsers without cloud dependency. The model, open‑source and designed for edge deployment, could support lightweight assistant or personalization workloads on end‑user machines.
news.enterprise_use: Check your internal dev environment for opportunities to integrate the Woof model into local assistant features or custom on‑prem voice solutions. Inaction means missing a low‑cost, privacy‑preserving alternative to cloud speech APIs for end‑user devices.

news.title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
news.source_text:
ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation
Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.
To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.
Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.
Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.
ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.
Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.
How ToyBlocks works
Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.
As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.
Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.
Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.
A physical robot gripper
news.summary: Hugging Face has released ToyBlocks, a controlled simulation framework that lets researchers automatically generate tasks and training demonstrations for robot arm manipulation. The platform emphasizes repeatable experiments, realistic physics, and scalability for studying learning dynamics.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on ToyBlocks for future integration opportunities if your organization explores robotic automation or AI-driven process optimization. Evaluate whether the framework could be adapted to simulate internal workflow scenarios or test new automation scripts before deployment.

news.title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
news.summary_raw: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed…
news.source_text:
I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
The startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes. They still need lots of human guidance, but they’re learning.
I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.
I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.
Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.
But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.
With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.

news.title: Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates
news.summary_raw: Australian universities are expanding access to ChatGPT and bringing AI into teaching and learning to prepare students for an AI-enabled workforce.
news.source_text:
Australian universities are creating AI-native graduates
The future of Australia’s workforce is taking shape before today’s students receive their degrees. Across university campuses, students are using AI to investigate ideas, build assistants and turn concepts into working prototypes. They are beginning to develop the skills they will take into research, established industries and ventures of their own.
Recognising this shift, Australian universities, including UNSW Sydney, University of Sydney, La Trobe University, and Adelaide University are forging collaborations with OpenAI to give their students and staff access to frontier AI tools.
Students, educators and IT teams are putting AI to work in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects that build pathways into industry. Alongside this work, universities are developing frameworks for where and how AI can be used in learning and assessment, helping students build practical skills while knowing when to rely on their own judgment. For teachers, employers and industry practitioners, these examples offer practical lessons in designing AI-supported learning, setting clear expectations for AI use and preparing Australians for an AI-enabled workplace.
New research* commissioned by OpenAI reveals what students want from their universities, including the access to AI they increasingly expect. In a survey of more than 1,000 Australian university students, 81% said they already use AI several times a week, including more than a third (33%) who use it multiple times a day. Over a quarter (28%) had already built an AI agent or assistant to help manage their studies, work or personal life. Four out of five students (79%) want their university to offer more opportunities to use advanced AI tools on real-world projects, with the same proportion interested in applying AI to challenges in health, climate, science or cyber security.
AI use and career readiness

- 61%Believe AI skills will be essential to success in their chosen career

Students also see those experiences as preparation for what comes next. More than sixty percent (61%) believe AI skills will be essential to success in their chosen career, and 65% believe those skills will give Australian graduates an advantage in the global workforce. There is entrepreneurial ambition, too. More than three quarters (76%) of students surveyed said they were interested in starting a company or working for themselves, while over two thirds (68%) believed AI would make it easier to start a business.

news.summary: Australian universities are partnering with OpenAI to give students and staff access to cutting‑edge AI tools, integrating AI into learning, research, and industry projects. The initiative reflects a broader trend of embedding AI literacy into higher education to prepare graduates for an AI‑enabled workforce.
news.enterprise_use: Monitor your university’s or organization’s AI adoption plans and evaluate how similar collaborations could enhance staff training or student projects. news.title: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking
news.summary_raw: An experiment in which AI models were asked to break into simulated networks showed the hacking skills of DeepSeek and GLM to be not far behind OpenAI’s most advanced cyber model, which isn’t public.
news.source_text:
Open-weight artificial intelligence models are now almost as capable of hacking into computer networks as the best closed ones, according to new research that heralds a much-anticipated turning point in the cybersecurity landscape.
Vals, a company that measures AI capabilities, set out to test how well different AI models could carry out complex, multi-step network instructions on mock corporate networks.
“The best frontier models, locked up inside the labs and available only through trusted access programs, are now starting to be matched by open models that anybody can download,” says Nikil Ravi, a researcher at Vals.
The company’s findings suggest that closed models no longer have a definitive edge in cyber skills, meaning recent efforts by frontier labs to limit access to their models, and thereby slow the proliferation of such capabilities, may potentially be moot.
The findings are also noteworthy given that the US frontier labs, particularly Anthropic, premised the limited release of new models—beginning with Claude Mythos Preview in April—on the idea that gated access would only buy time before advanced hacking capabilities were broadly available.
Anthropic's frontier red team lead, Logan Graham, told WIRED in April that the company’s Project Glasswing, which gives trusted access to the full capabilities of new models, was focused on getting those tools “in the hands of defenders to give a head start.”
“We need to prepare now for a world where these capabilities are broadly available in 6, 12, 24 months. Many things would be different about security,” he told WIRED at the time.
Seven months later, that transition seems to have arrived on schedule.
Vals tested AI models in two simulated scenarios, giving them various specific tasks to achieve. The first scenario involved a mock corporate network accessible through a public-facing website. The second involved two different company networks; a model needed to compromise the first in order to gain access to the second.
The researchers found OpenAI’s most advanced cyber model, Daybreak, which is available only to trusted partners, to be the most capable, completing 81 percent of the tasks it was given in an average of two tests. The Chinese open-weight model DeepSeek was not far behind, completing 73 percent of the objectives on average. The Vals researchers note that on some tasks, the two models scored equally.
The research also showed how much cheaper it is to use an open-weight model for this kind of task. Vals says it costs $17 to $46 in tokens for GPT-6-Sol to carry out an attack compared to $2 to $3 for DeepSeek. Open models are generally cheaper because they can be run on one’s own hardware. Rayan Krishnan, CEO of Vals, says this also provides a strong incentive for those playing defense to use open models rather than proprietary ones.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Much of the year in cybersecurity has played out as predicted, with AI automating core hackin
news.summary: Open-weight AI models such as DeepSeek are now matching closed models in hacking capabilities, according to new research. This means attackers could use cheaper, publicly available models to breach corporate networks, forcing a reassessment of existing security controls.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Review your current perimeter and endpoint defenses for vulnerabilities that AI could exploit, and consider integrating AI-based threat detection tools. S2: Failure to update defenses now could expose your network to automated, multi-step attacks that bypass traditional controls. S3: This directly impacts your MDM, endpoint security, and SSO configurations.

news.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
news.summary_raw: Certain configurations of Alpine are affected. Other distros may be as well.
news.source_text:
Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.
The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.
One connection, works every time, needs no retries
There are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a “*” in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.
When all the conditions are met, the consequences are high.
“An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password,” Alpine maintainers said Thursday. “It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.”
When logging into a passwordless account, the attacker can gain access by inputting more than 256 characters in the password field.
Security firm Checkpoint said that the use of the SHA256 or SHA512 functions “matters because sshd borrows that account’s salt. Without it, the attack fails.” Company researchers said their testing also showed that the account must be active, not just hold a hash. Checkpoint further reported that root accounts are safe under the default PermitRootLogin prohibit password setting, though reachable accounts with doas or sudo rights can still become root.
news.summary: A decade-old flaw in Alpine Linux’s OpenSSH-mu­sl configuration allows attackers to SSH in without a password if specific conditions are met. The issue exploits passwordless accounts and SHA256/512 hashed passwords, enabling remote takeover with a single connection.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Inspect all servers using Alpine or musl-based distributions—verify if SSH uses PAM or has passwordless accounts with SHA256/512 hashes and update the sshd_config to disable passwordless logins. S2: Failure to patch exposes any device reachable via SSH to immediate credential‑less compromise. S3: This directly impacts any cloud or edge devices managed through JumpCloud or MDM where Alpine images are deployed.

news.title: Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems
news.summary_raw: OpenAI is partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities, test connections with third-party services, and strengthen defenses with frontier AI.
news.source_text:
Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems
Today we’re announcing a partnership with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems. Our engineers and Hacktron’s security researchers will choose high-priority areas to test together, with a focus on how our systems interact with third-party services. As part of the partnership, we’re expanding Hacktron’s access to our frontier models through Daybreak Red.
As we work to accelerate cyber defense with frontier AI, we’re applying the same urgency to finding and fixing vulnerabilities in our own systems. Earlier this week, we announced that Cathedral’s researchers will work alongside our teams in our next security sprint. We also raised our bug bounty rewards to give independent researchers more reason to pursue vulnerabilities our own testing may have missed.
We became familiar with Hacktron through our Security Bug Bounty program and were impressed by the impact of the vulnerabilities its researchers have discovered and disclosed to us. The team builds AI agents for code review, penetration testing, and red teaming. Their research(opens in a new window) has uncovered vulnerabilities in how applications, cloud infrastructure, and identity systems interact. Their work shows what’s possible when security engineers build around AI to move faster and take on more ambitious research.
As AI agents connect services in new ways, that combination of skills becomes even more valuable. Working alongside Hacktron will help us test those connections more deeply and use what we learn to strengthen our defenses.
We’re grateful to Hacktron and other independent researchers who put time into finding and reporting weaknesses to help strengthen the security that protects all our users. To see which systems are in scope or submit a finding, visit our Security Bug Bounty program(opens in a new window).
news.summary: OpenAI has partnered with Hacktron to aggressively hunt for vulnerabilities in its systems, especially where AI models interact with third‑party services. The collaboration expands Hacktron’s access to OpenAI’s frontier models and aims to surface security gaps faster than traditional testing.
news.enterprise_use: 1. Go to your OpenAI or other AI platform’s bug‑bounty portal this week and verify that the new vulnerability‑scanning rules are applied to all cloud‑integrated services you rely on. 2. Failure to do so could expose your organization to unseen weaknesses in the AI components that feed your workflows. 3. The most relevant tool here is your SSO/identity provider (e.g., Okta, Azure AD) because the partnership specifically targets identity‑system interactions.

news.title: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails
news.summary_raw: Data brokers are collecting all sorts of internal corporate files to help train AI models. Not everyone is thrilled.
news.source_text:
Lately a new kind of pitch has found its way into my inbox. “Not sure if you've heard,” writes someone named Nick, “but AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI are paying media companies such as Wired $350K to $1.8M as a one time fee for a copy of their old work records (documents, emails, slack messages, tickets, etc.) for training better models.”
Another email with a similar pitch (adding call transcripts to the list of desired information) raised the stakes to a possible $2 million. “Public data is exhausted, and the labs are spending over $45B on private data to build better models,” writes someone named Cora.
While I was aware that AI companies are buying expert data from various sources, there hasn’t been that much attention paid to it. But once I looked into it, I discovered that this business is way bigger than I suspected—and according to its practitioners, it could have as much impact on workers and society as the data centers that are dominating the news these days.
The companies that contacted me are part of an industry boom in data acquisition that’s been quietly buying the workflows of sizable companies and is still so hungry that it’s bleeding into our inboxes. A freelance writer recently wrote about her experience with a company called Handshake, which offered her $1,000 for her work on a single story. (She didn’t sell.) A representative from Handshake confirmed the offer to me: “We license professional documents across a lot of fields so the labs can test and train how models handle real knowledge work,” he said. “Journalism is one of those fields.” Handshake tells me that a big part of its business is buying graduate students’ papers and coursework.
An entrepreneur friend of mine tells me he’s been getting mail from multiple companies whose business is “helping startups wind down their companies," as one email from a company named Sunset explained it. “We handle the full process, scrubbing and anonymizing the data so the company people and any identifying details are stripped out, then brokering the deal with the labs.”
Those newer data acquisition startups are hoping to achieve the quick success of the dominant companies in the field, which themselves are only a few years old. Industry leaders Handshake, Micro1, and Mercor are snapping up databases as if it were a modern gold rush. The industry leader seems to be Mercor, founded in 2023; last year its three cofounders became billionaires at 22. Like all the companies, it claims to have partnerships with just about all the major AI labs. (The response from the companies themselves was more circumspect: Anthropic acknowledges that there’s a big market for data, but told me that it doesn’t buy workflow from live companies like WIRED. OpenAI didn’t come up with a response before publication.)
In an interview, Mercor CEO Brendan Foody told me that the market is poised to explode as the AI industry seeks dramatically more data. Mercor originally started as an AI recruiting company, but
news.summary: AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI are paying media companies large sums to acquire internal work files, emails, and other documents for model training. This data‑acquisition trend poses significant privacy and security risks for organizations that store sensitive communications in tools like Google Workspace, JumpCloud, and Freshservice.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Review your Google Workspace and JumpCloud settings this week to ensure that internal documents and email archives are flagged as confidential and that access controls are strictly enforced. S2: If these files are exposed, AI labs could ingest them, potentially creating data leakage and compliance violations. S3: This directly impacts your Google Workspace, JumpCloud, and Freshservice environments where sensitive data is stored and managed.

news.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent
news.summary_raw: Meta's Muse agents continue to get new features and integrations. Spaces promises to be a new way to interact with the AI helpers.
news.source_text:
Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.
As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.
For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice, which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot, which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.
news.summary: Meta has launched "Spaces", a new feature that lets users create topic‑specific breakout conversations with their Muse AI agents and integrate third‑party apps for real‑time updates. This adds a new layer of contextual collaboration to Meta’s AI ecosystem, enabling more targeted project management and data sync within the agent interface.
news.enterprise_use: S1: In the next 30 days, monitor the adoption of Meta Spaces and evaluate whether the integration of third‑party app data could be replicated in your internal tools to streamline project workflows. S2: Not leveraging this kind of context‑aware collaboration could mean missing out on efficient, AI‑driven project tracking that your team might otherwise build from scratch.

news.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
news.summary_raw: Company said a "multifront cyberattack" included AI agents and an on-path data snatch.
news.source_text:
Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security.
The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and public sources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It’s unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats.
We regret to inform you…
Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It’s not clear why the company considered such information “non-sensitive.”
In a Wednesday update, the company said that part of the “ongoing multifront cyberattack” involved an “on-path attack” that exposed a subset of customer passwords, and that the attack vector had been identified and fixed. Also known as an adversary-in-the-middle attack, on-path attacks happen when a hacker gains access to a piece of infrastructure sending traffic back and forth between two parties. Chainalysis has yet to say where the infrastructure compromise occurred and if the data obtained from it was TLS encrypted.
news.summary: Chainalysis, a blockchain analysis firm, confirmed that attackers used AI agent‑assisted techniques to steal sensitive credentials and tokens from all of its users, including high‑profile government and corporate clients. The breach, disclosed just last Friday, exposed user identities, password hashes, and active tokens, raising immediate security concerns across the industry.
news.enterprise_use: S1: Review your organization’s use of blockchain analytics tools and audit any integrations with Chainalysis or similar services for exposed credentials. S2: Failure to do so risks credential reuse attacks and insider threats, especially if your team relies on Chainalysis for compliance or fraud detection. S3: Pay particular attention to any Google Workspace, JumpCloud, or Azure AD connections that pull data from Chainalysis, as those could be vectors for credential compromise.

news.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
news.summary_raw: OpenAI has reportedly raised an additional $11 billion as part of a funding round that hasn't closed yet but is expected to in the coming weeks.
news.source_text:
OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.
Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.
In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.
The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.
OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.
The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market, with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.
news.summary: OpenAI has secured an additional $11 billion in a funding round, valuing the company at $1.25 trillion, with the round expected to close in the coming weeks. The announcement follows earlier reports of a larger $30 billion target and highlights the company’s continued focus on growth and potential IPO plans.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on OpenAI’s funding trajectory as it may influence future API pricing or availability; monitor the OpenAI API dashboard for any upcoming changes that could impact cost or capacity for your Google Workspace and MDM integrations.

news.title: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://www.planned-obsolescence.org/p/ai-is-dramatically-accelerating-ai
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50397994
Points: 117

news.source_text:
This post discusses a public METR report on AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic. I did not work on this project or see the unredacted report.1 All opinions are my own and do not represent METR or the report authors.
Thanks to Ryan Greenblatt for discussion, feedback, and help with modeling, and Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, and Hjalmar Wjik for comments.
Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026), say this threshold will be met when:
- They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D.2 
- This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs.3 
For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed.4
The report authors found that:
- Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative." 
- While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted. 
This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack. Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team) have projected.
Researchers must be sped up a whole lot
Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that.
Researchers work on improving algorithms and architectures; Anthropic has sometimes referred to these innovations as “compute multipliers.”5 Overall AI capabilities (“effective compute”) is the product of compute multipliers and training compute. Because the compute multipliers are only one input into capabilities, this means that if AI capabilities are advancing twice as fast overall because of software progress, the rate of growth in compute multipliers would need to be more than twice as fast: perhaps ~2.5-3x faster based on reasonable assumptions.6 Since the
news.summary: Anthropic’s latest Responsible Scaling Policy indicates that AI-driven automation has already doubled their research capabilities progress, signaling a rapid acceleration in AI development. This finding underscores the potential for shorter timelines in AI breakthroughs, raising concerns about future security and compliance implications.
news.enterprise_use: Monitor Anthropic’s public disclosures and related AI policy updates for emerging risk signals; incorporate findings into your organization’s AI governance reviews and adjust security postures accordingly. Early awareness can help preempt policy shifts that may affect compliance requirements across your Google Workspace, JumpCloud, and other SSO/MDM ecosystems.

news.title: A Jev that can ask Opus for help gives Opus accuracy at 4x lower cost
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://hightouch.com/blog/llm-judges-identity-resolution
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50397429
Points: 230
# Comments: 50
news.source_text:
We wanted to test whether LLMs and decision models, specifically Jev and Luna, could solve a hard problem that we encounter regularly (grading identity resolution results). We found that while both models performed okay out of the box (88.8–97.3% accuracy), implementing a hybrid model that combines Jev + Opus achieves frontier accuracy at > 4x lower costs.
Our other findings:
- Luna performs better than Jev out of the box, but the gap disappears on harder cases.
- Jev's confidence is better calibrated. Most of its mistakes come with low confidence its right. Most of Luna's mistakes come with high confidence. This enables Jev to perform better than Luna in a hybrid model harness.
- Frontier models are still more accurate than decision models
- Decision models are up to 90× cheaper and more than 10× faster out of the box. They cost $0.5 - $0.10 per 1,000 identities and answer in about 0.15 seconds, but trail Opus accuracy by about 6 percentage points on harder benchmarks.
What is identity resolution?
Identity resolution is the process of mapping data to corresponding real people. More precisely, say you have a set of data records D. Determine a set of identities I and mapping m(D)->I such that each record d ∈ D maps to an identity i ∈ I , each i corresponds to exactly one real person in the real world, and no two i correspond to the same person in the real world.
This is foundational for any company wishing to do outreach, personalization, or analytics on customers. You can’t know, for instance, the lifetime value of a customer without being able to map all their purchases to a single identity.
For example, the input data might contain the following records. IDR would ideally create one identity, Alice, and associate all of these records with Alice.
In practice, IDR is very difficult. People share emails, move addresses, etc. There might also be errors in the data. See some examples here:
The most common and problematic issue with IDR is over-merging. This is when an identity i incorrectly corresponds to multiple people in the real world.
Detecting over-merging
On real data, there is no answer key we can consult after we’ve merged records into identities. If there were, then we'd just use that to match data, and we wouldn't need to do IDR. This makes it very difficult to assess the accuracy of any IDR algorithm. In practice, teams will spend months attempting to determine if their IDR is working.
You can use heuristics to look for statistical signs of over-merged profiles (count the number of emails per identity, etc), but ultimately you need to sample output identities and review them by hand to know how well your IDR algorithm is performing.
To do this, we define the records Dᵢ as the set of d such that m(d) -> i for any given i. If the IDR engine is successful, then we should only find evidence of one real person in any given Dᵢ.
Human sampling is slow (~50 identities/hr), and sampling small numbers of identities gives poor estimates of over-mer
news.summary: A hybrid AI model combining Jev and Opus achieves higher identity resolution accuracy at a quarter of the cost compared to using Opus alone. The study highlights that decision models are cheaper and faster, but less accurate on complex cases.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on the Jev+Opus hybrid approach as it may improve customer data mapping accuracy in your organization’s analytics or CRM systems. Evaluate the cost/accuracy trade‑off for your identity‑resolution workflows within the next 30 days to determine if an investment in this hybrid model could reduce manual data cleaning effort and improve personalization.

news.title: Measuring how AI agents handle everyday wet-lab science
news.summary_raw: OpenAI introduces BioBasicsBench, a 100-task benchmark measuring how well AI agents interpret raw experimental data and handle everyday wet-lab science.
news.source_text:
Measuring how AI agents handle everyday wet-lab science
Introducing BioBasicsBench, a benchmark measuring how well AI agents interpret raw experimental data across 100 routine wet-lab tasks.
Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. As part of that mission, we want to help scientists accelerate biological research—from understanding disease to developing new treatments. For AI agents to contribute, they need to reliably interpret the experimental evidence scientists work with every day in wet labs, where they run experiments with biological samples. Everyday wet-lab work involves failed experiments, ambiguous images and conflicting observations. Existing benchmarks are built around charts and images selected for scientific papers may miss this ambiguity and the troubleshooting it requires. That’s why we’re introducing BioBasicsBench, a new benchmark developed with Ligo, a biotech company focused on enzyme design, to measure how well agents handle routine wet-lab analysis.
The benchmark’s 100 tasks test whether agents can interpret raw experimental data, identify errors, and recognize when the evidence cannot support a conclusion. Getting these tasks right matters because misreading an image or overlooking a problem with the controls used to check an experiment’s results can lead scientists to draw the wrong conclusion and spend time on experiments that won’t help answer their question.
At the ‘xhigh’ setting, which allows more reasoning per task, GPT‑6 Astra earned an average of 66.7% of the available credit, compared with 43.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. The results show progress on routine lab analysis, with room for further improvements in interpreting images, checking controls and applying experimental context.
BioBasicsBench uses raw experimental evidence, from gel images and colony plates to microscopy and instrument readouts.
BioBasicsBench has 100 tasks across five areas of routine wet-lab work: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. Tasks range from simple requests, such as reading the molecular weight of a DNA sample in a gel, to detailed assay analysis, but all involve routine work that wet-lab scientists should be able to complete reliably.
Scientists created the tasks using data from their own experiments, pairing each question with expert-written grading criteria. Each task underwent an internal review by a Ligo scientist who had not written it, an external review by a PhD-level scientist working in a wet lab, and a final internal review.
Agents return a structured answer with the requested conclusion, measurement or recommendation and, where required, supporting reasoning. Answers receive credit against individual rubric criteria, allowing the benchmark to distinguish a correct conclusion from a partially correct analysis. news.summary: OpenAI has released BioBasicsBench, a benchmark that tests AI agents’ ability to interpret raw experimental data from wet‑lab tasks such as gel images and microscopy readouts. The benchmark, developed with biotech partner Ligo, evaluates agents on 100 routine tasks, aiming to improve AI reliability in scientific research.
news.enterprise_use: Check if your organization’s AI tools or research workflows could integrate or benchmark against BioBasicsBench to ensure data‑interpretation accuracy before deployment. Ignoring this may mean continued reliance on less tested AI models that could misinterpret critical experimental data.
